name: Sweet Brown
lede: Sweet Brown is a warm, brick-leaning red-brown, named with the vague, appetite-driven modifier 'sweet,' and it is one of the more common named colors in our entire painting archive.

sections.title: A sweet-tasting red-brown
sections.body: Our graph classes this as a plant, food or landscape word — 'sweet,' used loosely rather than tied to any single fruit or spice — with no fuller account in the books we checked [1]. It is also drawn from [[brazil-red]] in our graph, with its real nearest look-alike being [[medium-carmine]], almost the same hue, and [[levant-red]] and [[reddish-brick]] close behind [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this red-brown in 382 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.61 percent, as photographed, with the within-painting lens counting 414 — more common than 81 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1400s, 6.8 percent of the 945 paintings we have from then (64 paintings), 3.2 times the museums' expected rate, and plays an accent in 91 percent of its appearances [3]. Its most devoted painter is Henri Matisse, in 6 of 50 works here, 5.0 times his own baseline, and it shares canvases with Persian Plum and Dark Sienna far more than chance would predict [3]. It is also most over-represented in paintings from India, 2.5 times expected [3].
